## Why use real examples as well as simulations?

Simulations reveal whether a method recovers a rule that we know. Real datasets
show what happens with rounding, missing observations, uneven distributions,
and relationships whose true form is unknown. Both are useful tests, with
different lessons.

Start with the getting-started vignette if you are new to R or `binwise`.
This companion guide uses three historical datasets supplied with R. No data
files, accounts, optional data packages, or paper-specific objects are needed.
The examples execute when this guide is built. They are demonstrations of the
workflow, not a systematic benchmark or validation of every package feature.

```{r load-package}
library(binwise)
```

## 1. Landmass areas and a very long tail

`datasets::islands` contains areas of 48 large landmasses, measured in thousands
of square miles. It includes continents as well as islands and covers landmasses
above 10,000 square miles. R's documentation attributes it to the 1975 *World
Almanac and Book of Facts*. These are historical measurements of a selected set
of landmasses, not a random sample of all islands.
[Dataset documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/islands.html).

The original object is a named vector, so first turn it into a data frame.

```{r landmass-data}
landmasses <- data.frame(
  landmass = names(datasets::islands),
  area = as.numeric(datasets::islands)
)
head(landmasses)
landmass_comparison <- bin_compare(
  landmasses, "area", bins = 4, min_count = 2, min_prop = .01
)
plot(landmass_comparison, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
     xlab = "Area in thousands of square miles",
     main = "Very different landmasses can share a quantile bin",
     scheme_labels = c(quantile_4 = "Four quantile bins",
                       equal_width_4 = "Four equal-width bins"))
landmass_comparison$bins[, c("scheme", "bin", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

With only 48 observations, this descriptive example uses a count screen of two,
not the package default of 20. That does not make two observations adequate for
statistical inference. It simply makes the chosen warning rule explicit.

**Look for** the broad upper quantile interval and the imbalance of equal-width
counts. Quantiles can balance counts while grouping very different areas.
Equal widths can preserve absolute size distinctions but leave small groups.
A log-scale display is another way to inspect the distribution while retaining
the numeric measurements.

**Conclusion.** This reproduces the long-tail problem in real data. With no
outcome in this example, it cannot tell us whether bins improve prediction.

## 2. Geyser durations and apparent clusters

`datasets::faithful` contains 272 observations of eruption duration and waiting
time until the next eruption at Old Faithful. Both are measured in minutes.
The R documentation notes substantial rounding of eruption times and the
existence of other versions of these data. Use this version consistently when
reproducing the example.
[Dataset documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/faithful.html).

```{r geyser-scatter}
geyser <- datasets::faithful
plot(geyser$eruptions, geyser$waiting, pch = 16, col = "#397985",
     xlab = "Eruption duration in minutes",
     ylab = "Waiting time to the next eruption in minutes")
```

The plot suggests shorter and longer eruptions. For an exploratory descriptive
summary, compare quartiles with a three-minute boundary.

```{r geyser-bins}
geyser_comparison <- bin_compare(
  geyser, "eruptions", methods = "quantile",
  custom_breaks = list(three_minutes = c(min(geyser$eruptions), 3,
                                        max(geyser$eruptions)))
)
plot(geyser_comparison, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
     xlab = "Eruption duration in minutes", main = "Describing short and long eruptions",
     scheme_labels = c(quantile_4 = "Four quantile bins",
                       three_minutes = "Exploratory three-minute boundary"))
geyser_groups <- bin_apply(
  geyser, geyser_comparison$diagnoses$three_minutes, name = "duration_group"
)
table(geyser_groups$duration_group)
```

**Conclusion.** A short/long summary can be useful for communication, but three
minutes here is an exploratory choice. We have not established a physical
threshold or that waiting time is constant within each category. Clusters in a
predictor are not enough to establish a step-shaped outcome relationship.
Rounding also creates ties that should stay together.

These are observations of one geyser over time. A random row split would not
by itself establish performance for future eruptions. This section deliberately
makes a descriptive claim only.

## 3. Air quality, missing values, and held-out months

`datasets::airquality` contains 153 daily observations from New York between
May and September 1973. Ozone is measured in parts per billion, temperature in
degrees Fahrenheit, wind in miles per hour, and solar radiation in Langleys.
The original sources are the New York State Department of Conservation and
the National Weather Service.
[Dataset documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/airquality.html).

We will predict ozone from temperature, wind, and solar radiation. Only the
representation of temperature changes between models. We compare a linear
temperature term, a natural cubic spline, and quartile categories.

```{r air-missingness}
air <- datasets::airquality
needed <- c("Ozone", "Temp", "Wind", "Solar.R")
colSums(is.na(air[, needed]))
sum(complete.cases(air[, needed]))
```

There are 111 complete observations for this comparison. The remaining 42
rows are excluded because at least one required measurement is missing.
Complete-case evaluation can describe a selected subset; this example does
not solve the missing-data problem.

Keep all observations from a month together and leave one month out at a time.
The models train on the other four months. The quartile cutpoints are learned
using training observations only, including when a held-out temperature is
outside the training range. Automatic quantile recipes extend their outermost
intervals to cover such values; their internal cutpoints stay training-derived.

```{r air-validation}
air_check <- bin_validate(
  air, outcome = "Ozone", variables = "Temp",
  controls = c("Wind", "Solar.R"),
  schemes = list(quartiles = list(Temp = list(probs = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1)))),
  group = "Month", folds = 5, seed = 12, reps = 0,
  spline_df = 3, reference = "spline"
)
air_check$scores
air_check$diagnostics
```

`reps = 0` omits bootstrap intervals. With only five month groups, this small
example is not a good setting for presenting cluster-bootstrap intervals as
precise evidence. `NA` in the interval columns means no interval was calculated.
All eligible test observations receive predictions from all three models.

The pooled RMSE is about 23.54 ppb for the linear temperature model,
21.44 ppb for temperature quartiles, and 21.05 ppb for the spline. The MAE
values are about 17.73, 15.84, and 14.66 ppb, respectively. Lower is better.
Quartiles improve on a linear temperature term, but the spline gives the lowest
pooled errors among these candidates. Check each held-out fold as well.

```{r air-folds}
air_check$fold_scores[air_check$fold_scores$metric == "RMSE", c("fold", "model", "n", "score")]
```

Quartiles have lower RMSE in each of the five held-out months, although the
size of improvement varies. Categories can improve
on a simple linear predictor on real observations while a flexible continuous
alternative does better overall. The spline need not win every individual fold.
This small comparison does not establish a stable performance ranking in new
settings.

**Limits of that conclusion.** There are just five months from one historical
summer, some observations are missing, and days may remain dependent across
month boundaries. Training includes months later than the held-out month, so
this is not a test of forecasting future months using only the past.
It is also not evidence that temperature categories cause ozone changes.
The included spline supplies one flexible continuous comparator. Its complexity
was specified in advance and its knots learned within each training fold.
A better score than a straight line does not identify a uniquely correct set
of thresholds.

## Related tools have different primary purposes

This is a targeted review of official documentation and primary research,
checked on 13 November 2026. It is not an exhaustive review or a performance
benchmark. These are adjacent tools with some shared techniques, not a list
of interchangeable packages. Software capabilities change.

| Tool | Established capability | Relationship to binwise |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [Base R `cut()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/cut.html) | Assigns numeric values to intervals and returns categories. | Basic bin creation is already available. `bin_apply()` connects assignment to saved diagnostic schemes. |
| [`dlookr`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=dlookr) | Data diagnosis, exploration, transformations, binning, and automated reports. | Shared diagnostic and binning features within a broader exploration package. binwise organizes these steps around evaluating a categorization decision. |
| [`rbin`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rbin) | Manual, quantile, equal-length, and other binning tools, with category creation and interactive add-ins. | An established alternative for constructing and inspecting bins. |
| [`interflex`](https://yiqingxu.org/packages/interflex/) | Estimates and diagnoses conditional marginal effects, with binning, kernel, linear, and other flexible estimators. | Uses bins to diagnose conditional effects across a moderator. binwise evaluates the consequences of replacing numeric predictors with categories, including comparisons without interactions. |
| [`binsreg`](https://github.com/nppackages/binsreg) | Binscatter regression, inference, plotting, bin-number selection, and specification tests. | Related estimation methodology, rather than a direct substitute for this decision workflow. Partitions support curve estimation and inference, including variation within bins. |
| [`cutpointr`](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v098i11) | Estimates cutpoints for binary classification and evaluates stability and out-of-sample performance. | Demonstrates that choosing and validating cutpoints is established work. It targets a more specific classification problem. |

In particular, the classic `interflex` binning diagnostic estimates conditional
marginal effects and allows within-bin moderator terms. It is not merely a table
of outcome averages. `binsreg` estimates unknown relationships using partitions
and formal inference. Choosing partitions for curve estimation answers a
different question from choosing substantive categories for a variable.
[interflex binning diagnostic](https://yiqingxu.org/packages/interflex/02_classic.html),
[binsreg reference](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=binsreg).

None of these packages is required to run this guide. They should be acknowledged
and considered when their methods better match a user's research question.
The comparison above describes scope, not superiority. `binwise` currently fits
ordinary linear and binary logistic models, optionally with natural cubic
spline terms, in `bin_interact()`. It does not
supply the specialized estimators of these packages. Advanced callbacks in
`bin_validate()` let users bring their own fitting procedure.

## Where to go next

Choose a tool by the question you need to answer. These packages can complement
`binwise`; this guide does not claim that it reproduces their methods.

| If you need to... | Consider | What goes beyond the current binwise interface |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Diagnose a whole dataset, investigate missing values or outliers, and compare transformations | [dlookr](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=dlookr) | Broad exploration, transformation, and automated reporting. |
| Estimate how a treatment's marginal effect varies across a moderator and diagnose interaction assumptions | [interflex](https://yiqingxu.org/packages/interflex/) | Specialized conditional-effect estimators and inference, including support diagnostics. |
| Estimate regression curves with binscatter, construct uniform confidence bands, or test shape restrictions | [binsreg](https://github.com/nppackages/binsreg) | Formal binscatter estimation, inference, and partition selection. binwise's plotted bands are pointwise model-based mean intervals. |
| Estimate and validate a cutoff for classifying a binary outcome | [cutpointr](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v098i11) | Classification-specific cutoff optimization, stability assessment, and validation. binwise does not optimize cutpoints against the outcome. |
| Use weight-of-evidence summaries or interactive bin-construction add-ins | [rbin](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rbin) | Tools oriented to constructing and evaluating such binning schemes. |

Read each package's assumptions and documentation before choosing it. None of
these options removes the need to define the analytical question, preserve honest
validation, and interpret what the resulting estimates mean. The packages are
suggested resources here, not dependencies installed automatically by binwise.

## What the research says

**Arbitrary categorization can be costly.** Altman and Royston explain how
splitting a continuous measurement can discard information, reduce power,
and obscure differences within groups. They also warn against choosing a
cutpoint because it yields the most impressive result. This supports retaining
numeric originals and making the rationale for cutpoints explicit.
[Altman and Royston (2006), *The cost of dichotomising continuous variables*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1458573/).

**Equal counts do not imply similar outcomes.** Bennette and Vickers show why
quantile categories can impose implausibly constant risk within broad intervals,
especially in tails. They advocate flexible continuous relationships and
meaningful comparisons. They also distinguish exploratory categorization from
using categories as the principal analysis.
[Bennette and Vickers (2012), *Against quantiles*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3353173/).

**Binning can help diagnose interaction assumptions.** Hainmueller, Mummolo,
and Xu examine failures of linear interaction assumptions and inadequate
common support. Their binning and kernel comparisons help check whether a
simple interaction is credible in regions with sufficient observations. These
are diagnostics for a particular statistical question, not a general instruction
to categorize every continuous variable.
[Hainmueller, Mummolo, and Xu (2019), *How Much Should We Trust Estimates from Multiplicative Interaction Models?*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/how-much-should-we-trust-estimates-from-multiplicative-interaction-models-simple-tools-to-improve-empirical-practice/D8CAACB473F9B1EE256F43B38E458706).

**Bins also support formal nonparametric methods.** Cattaneo, Crump, Farrell,
and Feng develop statistical foundations for binscatter estimation, inference,
and choosing the number of bins. This is a distinct use of bins from assuming
a handful of fixed categories fully describes an outcome relationship.
The existence of a rigorous binscatter method does not validate arbitrary
thresholds in a different model.
[Cattaneo and colleagues (2024), *On Binscatter*](https://nppackages.github.io/references/Cattaneo-Crump-Farrell-Feng_2024_AER.pdf).

**Cutpoint validation is established practice.** Thiele and Hirschfeld explain
how choosing an apparently optimal classification cutoff can exaggerate
performance. Their `cutpointr` package includes robust estimation and validation
methods. Selection and evaluation need to be separated, a principle that also
motivates training-only bin recipes and honest evaluation in `binwise`.
[Thiele and Hirschfeld (2021), *cutpointr*](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v098i11).

## A credible role for binwise

Our assessment is that the potential contribution is an accessible, connected
workflow for making and documenting a binning decision. That includes plain
language, counts next to ranges, explicit treatment of meaningful zeros and
signed values, saved reusable schemes, and shared-sample prediction comparisons.
It should help users discover when categorization is unhelpful as readily as
when it is useful.

The distinction from `dlookr` is purpose and organization. Its broad exploration
and transformation workflow includes useful binning functions. `binwise` is
organized around evaluating whether categorization serves a stated analytical
purpose, including what happens when the numeric predictor is retained in a
flexible form. That distinction does not make the individual techniques new.

This is a product and teaching contribution, not evidence that binning,
interaction diagnostics, or held-out evaluation are new statistical methods.
The individual techniques are established. Any claim of methodological novelty
would need a specific new statistical contribution and a focused comparison.
The distinct purpose of this workflow should be assessed on its own merits. Beginner
usability testing and broader comparisons of the implemented alternatives
would be useful next steps before a public release.

## Reproducibility

All three real datasets remain in R's `datasets` package; this guide does not
redistribute separate copies. The code uses their documented versions and
records the session below. The supplied simulated examples are described in
`?binwise_examples` and `?binwise_interaction`.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
